lines.text: for which we bear responsibility? Are not these obligations
arising from our tasks in life and from our relations with our
own, part and parcel of our very life? Ought we to seek
release from them in order to gain divine freedom? At the
present time should we repudiate our anxieties about our
relations and friends who are fighting for us in dire distress
and danger? Ought we to forget the sorrow that we bear in
our hearts concerning those who have been taken from us?
Our compassion with so many a one who is deeply afflicted?
Would not the attainment of a freedom in which we are no
longer moved by all this, amount to a subtle technique of
withdrawing from the network of human relations, of
retiring within oneself in a state of self-chosen isolation and
seclusion, of rigid insensibility—we might even say inner
deadness?
This cannot be what is meant by the words of Jesus.
Otherwise He would not have been able to add that on
"that day" we are still to pray and address our petitions to
God. No! His promise concerns precisely those who stand
involved in the complex relations of life, for in His high-
priestly prayer He prays to God for His own: "I do not pray
that Thou shouldst take them out of the world, but that
Thou shouldst keep them from the evil one" (John 17: 15).
It is not from the encounters of life that we should seek free-
dom but from ourselves; from the fact that in all these
encounters we seek our own interests, holding fast to our-
selves. Freedom from ourselves means a radical surrender
of ourselves to God, and hence readiness for all that God
sends us: openness to all the encounters of life.
III
But one thing is certainly true: if we wish to experience the
joy of freedom which marks "that day".
